brewing.notes: A common starting point for herbal infusions: boiling water, about five minutes.

description:
A Ugandan non-alcoholic drink of pineapple peel and fruit boiled with ginger and tea leaves, served hot or chilled. The name comes from the Luganda word for pineapple.

Brew it as you would other herbal infusions. If the plant is new to you, check that it is safe for you first, especially when pregnant or on medication.
history: It is credited to the Baganda, who combined pineapple with tea leaves. Small vendors sell it from kiosks in suburban areas, sometimes in polythene bags, with stronger demand in hot seasons, and a packaged iced version was reported in 2025.
processing: Pineapple flesh and peel are pounded, then boiled in water for about two hours until brown; grated ginger and tea leaves go in for a further 15 to 30 minutes, then it is cooled, strained and sweetened if wanted.
harvest_season: Depends on the plant and the place.
vintage_note: Herbal infusions are not sold by vintage: buy recent stock and use it within a year or so.
